title: Joel Clark - A Perfectly Ordinary Blaseball Experience
speaker: Joel Clark
description:
This talk is from the 2020 virtual Roguelike Celebration:
https://roguelike.club/event2020.html

Joel is a member of The Game Band, and built the simulation that governs blaseball. He's responsible for so much of the game's unique tone – there would be no York Silk without his name generator. His talk explains design methodology and attitudes towards procedural generation that lead the team in creating blaseball and embracing chaos.

Blaseball: https://www.blaseball.com/
Find Blaseball on Twitter: https://twitter.com/blaseball 
Find Joel on Twitter: https://twitter.com/joel_a_clark

chapters.title: The role of chaos in design

Why did we make this thing? -- we receive about. The simplest, quickest answer I can give is

make sense of just the chaos of the world that's been happening
and it has helped our studios start to find a path forward through it. I have just been thinking
a lot about chaos and learning a lot about it and that's what I want to share with you today.
I am going to say chaos enough times where it won't make sense to anybody but
deal with it. On base level, chase is just unpredictability. It is not being able to
predict or parse the outcome of a set of initial conditions and behaviors. It is something that
feels totally random even if it is not. Chaos theory would say it is not random. We just can't
parse it because we don't have enough information. This is more or less the scientific view of chaos
but I am paraphrasing and butchering it. We talk about chaos as being complete disorder. Like the
2020 news cycle where things are being thrown at you all of the time or like an explosion
or, you know, a storm with stuff flying around. We think about when we talk about chaos is disorder.
I have really changed my definition to something that happens on a more personal level. Chaos is
a personal emotional experience rather than this big phenomenon. The same system is going to feel
much more chaotic to one person versus another depending on your understanding and chaos.
Chaos is a moment to moment part of people's lives and a core part of what makes games interesting. I
wanted to find a definition to match that. Here is what I came up with. Chaos is discomfort caused by
trying to understand something. Particularly when failing or struggling to understand that thing.
And then I have been using that definition to reframe my own game design as we are exposing
players to chaos and then showing them path through it over and over. I think we are thinking
about that all of the time whether we phrase it that way in game design. We can talk about pacing,
introducing new systems and everything is going to be a little chaotic to that player
until they learn about it and understand it. If you have a new enemy or a boss with suddenly
a bunch of new weird attacks you are not going to understand what's going on. It is going to
be unpredictable until you get hit by it once, twice, lose a few times, and then you start to
recognize the patterns and then you settle in. Once you figure it out, it is no longer chaotic.
You under it and know how to beat it but that process from being exposed to that new information
and figuring it out is uncomfortable. That's chaos to me. Let's get into Blaseball. There is
a lot of of things that make Blaseball chaotic but I had to narrow it down for this talk. The
first two I think will be understandable to everybody here. The first one is randomness. There
is a lot of talk about how Blaseball is a random number generator with lore on top and I am here to
confirm that's a 100% correct. Randomness is just exciting. Blaseball definitely embraces it is.
It is inherently chaotic and something you can't understand. That's the purpose of chaos, really.
I think is the cheapest form of chaos you can add to the game. Adding randomness, procedural
generation is a great example. If you embrace randomness, you can add chaos pretty cheaply. The
next one emergence or emergent system design. I am sure everyone has a some frame of what this is
being the Roguelike Celebration. I am not going to dive too far into it because it has
been explored for decades and all day today and yesterday but the idea is when systems interact
it drives complexity of outcome through the roof and that will keep players on their toes and
learning and interpreting and therefore causing chaos. When systems interact, it is going to cause
such a level of complexity and chaos that you just really can't do just by scripting something.
You are going to create things that are unexpected for even you, the developer, and that is just
exciting. I will probably mention more and about how Blaseball is equally chaotic to me. Sports in
particular are perfect examples of emergent system design. They producing infinite outcomes based off
simple rules and fans tune in to revel in that chaos. That's a big part of why we lean
into baseball as a topic. Baseball is so simple but it generates so much unexpected behavior.
That was really the starting point. And then we get more specifically into Blaseball.
The third thing is improvisational design. We have promised a lot mere -- here. We have promised
weekly updates, continued mystery and change and weirdness and that forces us to think on our toes
constantly. We can't have too much of a filter in your design or else we would run out of time and
we wouldn't get any changes in. It really forces us to change our approach to designing in this
game. We work out of the subconscious and we have to try to stay in synch with one another so
our design meetings don't, you know, get stuck on something. We have to keep moving and keep moving.
We are really not afraid of getting ideas in that are bad or weird. The design of this game
is really raw because it has to be because we have to move fast and you can imagine how that could
create some chaos. We are watching the randomness cause of events and reacting along with you. When
things shake out in surprising weird ways we have to change course and embrace it. Similarly,
when the community comes up with a plot, when they take the systems that are in their hands,
and decide to do something really exciting and fun with it, we have to pick it up and run with
it with the best we can. We at least partially anticipate it usually. We thought well, if they --
what happens if they don't have any pitchers? We don't have to think about that.
But the community deciding to rally around it is something that we can't
expect. Yeah, we are having a dialogue every season because between developers
and community and that brings so much unpredictability to the experience.
You know? It is a little stressful but it is incredibly fun to build a game that way.
The last thing I will mention as a design rule that I have tried to enforce
and it will sound a little absurd or funny but we are OK with the game getting sloppy.
I want you to happen there is going to be a bunch more pictures of trash cans just appearing so if
you can picture that it will help everyone's experience of that. We are OK with the game
sloppy. We are OK with that and lean into it and sometimes it is a little intentional. So
we are not afraid to take risks and if the design of a system falls flat we are probably
not going to fix it. Is that weird? At least not right now. We are instead trying to address issues
by adding new systems on top of the old broken systems and adding another link between the two
and the old broken systems continue to exist in the background and continue to influence
the game and simulation. We are fixing problems essentially by adding more problems which is, you
know, hilarious especially if you are a designer who tries to design cleanly around things.
I think this adds so much chaos to the experience and it is very fun.
With Blaseball specially I think it is important there is an
influx of new things in order to keep up the sense of unpredictability, in order to allow
more things for the community to interpret and try to make sense of. We prioritize new over better
always and it is partially that we can't afford to the time to overhaul a broken system.
I think it is a lot harder to take a broken system and reshape or tear it down and rebuild it than it
